entries.topic: Belief vs data: perceptions of mobility, polls on the Dream, system justification, meritocracy belief, survivorship

claims.text: Alesina, Stantcheva and Teso (AER 2018), surveys Feb-Oct 2016 (US n=4,705; UK 2,148; France 2,148; Italy 2,143; Sweden 1,494): US respondents put the chance that a bottom-quintile child reaches the top quintile at 11.7% vs 7.8% actual; staying in the bottom 32.2% perceived vs 33.1% actual; Europeans underestimated upward mobility (about 11% actual) and overestimated staying at the bottom.

Alesina et al.: shown pessimistic information, both left- and right-leaning respondents became more pessimistic; only left-leaning respondents increased support for equality-of-opportunity policies; right-leaning respondents changed no policy support.

Kraus (2015) pre-registered replication, 763 MTurk adults: large overestimation of mobility (d=2.63; original Kraus & Tan JESP 2015 d=3.05); overestimates larger for 'people like me'; higher subjective social class, conservatism and youth predicted larger overestimates; income not significant. Kraus & Tan proposed limited knowledge and a motive to see society as fair.

Davidai and Gilovich (2015), 3,034 adults via Harris Poll plus 290 MTurk: Americans overestimate upward and underestimate downward mobility; poorer respondents and conservatives believed in more mobility.

Chambers, Swan and Heesacker (Psychological Science 2015), 410 adults: participants underestimated mobility and 56% wrongly believed it had declined; only 15% correctly said it was stable; liberals underestimated more.
WSJ/NORC 2023: 36% American dream still holds true, 45% once held true but not anymore, 18% never; PRRI 2012 53% and 2016 48% (different methodology).

Pew ATP, same question 'have achieved / on your way / out of reach for you': Dec 5-11 2022 30/37/31; Apr 8-14 2024 31/36/30; general question April 2024: still possible 53%, once possible but not anymore 41%, never 6%.

Pew April 2024 (n=8,709): still possible by income: upper 64%, middle 56%, lower 39%; by age 65+ 68%, under 50 42%; achieved personally: White 39%, Asian 34%, Hispanic 19%, Black 15%; on the way Black 48%, Hispanic 47%.
Pew August 2017: 36% achieved, 46% on the way, 17% out of reach.
Brookings (9 July 2026) on Gallup: satisfaction with opportunity to get ahead 52% in 2026; Republicans 85%, Democrats 24%, a record 61-point gap (previous largest 40 in 2019).

Jost et al. (2003): lower-income respondents more likely to say large income differences are needed to motivate effort; 'those who suffer the most also have the most to explain, justify, and rationalize'. Brandt (2013) large-scale test found no support for the status-legitimacy hypothesis; advantaged people as or more supportive of the system.
Mijs (2019), ~25 years of ISSP data: 'the more unequal a society, the more likely its citizens are to explain success in meritocratic terms'.

Bénabou and Tirole (QJE 2006): people are motivated to believe effort is rewarded; this belief affects labour supply as well as politics; 'American' equilibrium of just-world beliefs and laissez-faire vs 'European' equilibrium with more pessimism and larger welfare state.
BLS BED: private establishments born March 2013: 79.6% survived 1 year, 50.6% 5 years, 34.7% 10 years.

Sandel: meritocracy 'leads to hubris among the winners and humiliation for those who lose out'; politicians of both parties promised a degree would secure success; at top-100 selective colleges about 70% of students from wealthy families vs about 3% from the bottom quintile.

entries.topic: Both parties' rhetoric of the Dream and enacted policy records

claims.text: Earliest cited 'bootstraps' uses (1834 Workingman's Advocate; 1843; 1863) mocked absurd or impossible feats; the OED's first example of the self-reliance sense is Joyce's Ulysses (1922).
Reagan, 17 July 1980, Detroit: 'a great national crusade to make America great again!'

Bush, 2 September 2004: 'build an ownership society, because ownership brings security, and dignity, and independence'; 'In an ownership society, more people will own their health care plans'; homeownership 'at an all-time high'.

Obama, 13 July 2012, Roanoke: 'If you were successful, somebody along the line gave you some help'; 'Somebody invested in roads and bridges. If you've got a business, you didn't build that. Somebody else made that happen.'
Boehner, 15-16 September 2011: 'Job creators in America are essentially on strike.'
DREAM Act: House passed 216-198 in December 2010; Senate cloture failed 55-41 on 18 December 2010, five votes short of 60 (36 Republicans and 5 Democrats against).
Fifth Circuit, 17 January 2025: DACA unlawful, injunction narrowed to Texas, program 'remains largely intact'; about half a million recipients.

As of late April 2026: renewals accepted; new initial requests accepted but not processed; Texas recipients keep deportation protection but Judge Hanen had not issued the order ending their work authorization.
Clinton, 22 August 1996: 'Today we are ending welfare as we know it'; welfare to be 'a second chance, not a way of life'; said nutrition cuts 'too deep' and cuts for legal immigrants 'far too deep'.
CBPP: for every 100 families in poverty, 68 received AFDC/TANF cash in 1996 and 21 in 2023.

AEI (Weidinger, 24 July 2026): adult recipients fell from 4.38m (FY1995) to 1.30m (FY2002) and 570,000 (FY2024), caseload down 85%; Haskins: work among the most disadvantaged mothers rose almost 40% in four years from 1996; never-married mothers' real earnings roughly doubled; only 8% of TANF families in FY2024 met the work requirement.
Trump, 16 June 2015, announcement closed: '...and we will make America great again'; also 'They will never make America great again' of opponents.

entries.topic: Deaths of despair, overdoses, life expectancy by income, and the critics

claims.text: Case and Deaton (PNAS 2015): mortality of white non-Hispanics 45-54 fell about 2% a year 1978-98 then rose about 0.5% a year to 2013; 96,000 deaths 1998-2013 had the 1998 rate held; 488,500 had the prior decline continued; poisonings, suicide, liver disease; high school or less all-cause +22%; other rich countries and US Black and Hispanic midlife mortality kept falling.

Case and Deaton (2020 book): about 600,000 midlife deaths would have been avoided had the pre-1999 decline continued; blame job market, health insurance costs, patent monopolies. Henderson (Cato): with PCE deflator non-college white men's wages rose 4.5% 1979-2017 rather than falling 13%; disputes causal story.
NCHS (13 May 2026): provisional overdose deaths 69,973 in 2025 vs 81,313 in 2024, almost 14% decline, third consecutive annual decline; opioid-involved 55,296 to 44,564.

Chetty et al. (JAMA 2016): life expectancy at 40 gap between richest and poorest 1%: 14.6 years men, 10.1 women; 2001-2014 top 5% gained 2.34 (men) and 2.91 (women) years, bottom 5% 0.32 and 0.04; bottom-quartile life expectancy varied about 4.5 years by area; correlated with smoking, not with access to care or income inequality.
Ruhm (2018), county data 1999-2015: economic conditions explain 'less than one-tenth of the rise in drug and opioid-involved mortality rates'; the drug environment plays the main role.

entries.topic: Audit additions: DACA status Oct 2026; child tax credit record

claims.text: National Immigration Forum (updated 2 Oct 2026): 'As of July 1 2026, Judge Hanen has not issued a modified order' and has not taken steps to wind down DACA in Texas; the Fifth Circuit ruling of 17 Jan 2025 remains unimplemented; DOJ proposal of 29 Sept 2025 would end Texas recipients' work authorization; USCIS accepts but does not process initial requests and processes renewals only, slowly (125,282 renewals pending, a record)

CRS R41873 (Nov 2025): TCJA (P.L. 115-97) temporarily doubled the maximum child tax credit and raised the refundable amount from $1,000 to $1,400; P.L. 119-21 permanently raised the maximum from $2,000 to $2,200 per child, indexed; refundable portion 15% of earnings above $2,500, capped at $1,700 (2025); only about half of taxpayers with children and income under $10,000 received the credit in 2022 (TPC estimate)
